When engineers say Data Engineering interviews are tough, this is what they truly mean.

A recent candidate who appeared for a Data Engineer interview at PepsiCo shared questions that were far from theoretical — they were real-world, production-grade challenges.

These weren’t “write a query” type questions, but “build like you’re in production” kind of problems.

Here’s what came up across rounds 👇

SQL 
➡ Identify top 5 products by sales while handling ties efficiently
➡ Detect orders delayed beyond monthly averages
➡ Use a recursive CTE to fetch complete org hierarchy
➡ Keep only the latest record among millions — efficiently

Python 
➡ Read, transform, and write an 18GB CSV file daily
➡ Detect spikes or drops in data using 3σ anomaly detection
➡ Build customer frequency logic without using Pandas

Pyspark & Big Data 
➡ Solve the “small file” problem on S3
➡ Optimize joins on billion-row datasets
➡ Handle data skew while maintaining performance

Data Modeling 
➡ Implement SCD Type 2 logic for historical tracking
➡ Design a scalable global supply chain data model
➡ Merge schemas from multiple data sources cleanly

Cloud 
➡ Stream data live using Kafka and Spark
➡ Migrate 12TB of on-prem data to cloud with zero downtime

What this tells you:
Top companies don’t test syntax — they test system thinking.

They look for engineers who can design, optimize, and scale real-world data systems.

If you’re preparing for a data switch, stop memorizing queries.
Start thinking in terms of pipelines, performance, and architecture.

author: Sanjeev Kumar Sahoo
headline: Full Stack Developer | Java · Spring Boot · React.js | Microservices · Kafka · Redis | Agentic AI & LLM Integration (LangChain4j, RAG)
text:
“We reduced database load by 70% — without adding a single index.”

Most devs jump straight to “Add an index” when queries get slow.
But sometimes, it’s not the database that’s slow — it’s how you use it.

Here’s what we found (and fixed):


1. Repeated Reads from the Same Table

Our service was hitting the DB ~40 times per user session — for the same data.
✅ Solution: Added a 30-second in-memory cache (Caffeine/Redis).
→ 40 queries → 1 query.


2. Chatty API Pattern

Frontend was calling 5 different APIs that all queried the same table.
✅ Solution: Aggregated data at backend and returned a single payload.
→ 5 round trips → 1.


3. Poor Pagination

Frontend was fetching entire datasets just to show 10 rows.
✅ Solution: Applied LIMIT/OFFSET and lightweight projection (SELECT id, name).
→ Response size dropped from 2MB → 80KB.


The Result

🚀 70% less DB load
💰 Infra bill down by 40%
⚡ Average response time: 600ms → 150ms


Real takeaway

Most performance issues aren’t about “bad queries.”
They’re about bad data flow.
If you reduce calls, you reduce load — instantly.

Have you ever solved a scaling issue without touching indexes or queries?

author: Sarita Jha
headline: Data Engineering Leader
text:
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(column) - The Great Counting Myth

If you've worked with SQL long enough, you've probably heard this one:
 
"Never use COUNT(*); it's inefficient."

Sounds logical, right? After all, that * looks like it's counting every single column. But here's the twist, it doesn't.

COUNT(*) simply counts rows, not columns.
It's the database equivalent of counting people in a room, no questions asked, no forms checked.

COUNT(column), on the other hand, is pickier.
It only counts rows where that column has a non-null value.
Think of it as counting how many people brought popcorn to movie night. No popcorn? You don't get counted.

And here's the interesting part - in most modern databases, COUNT(*) is actually faster than COUNT(column).
Why? Because it doesn't need to inspect any column values. It can rely on metadata or index-only scans to get the row count efficiently.

Use COUNT(*) when you want to count rows. It's clean, correct, and optimized.
Use COUNT(column) when NULLs matter and you only want non-empty values.

Zoom in and enjoy the SQL Sunflower — your quick interview refresher 🌻

Preparing for SQL interviews can feel overwhelming when concepts start to blend together. This cheat-sheet brings the most commonly tested SQL topics into one visual — perfect for quick revision before your next technical screen.

What you’ll find inside:
 • SELECT + WHERE — the foundation of every query
 • ORDER BY + GROUP BY + HAVING — the core of analytical questions
 • JOINS — most interview questions live here
 • Window Functions — RANK, LAG, LEAD, PARTITION BY
 • Subqueries & CTEs — for layered logic tasks
 • CASE, SET operations, and filtering tricks
 • Aggregation & Interview-style patterns

If you’re preparing for Data Analyst, BI, Data Science or Backend interviews — spend a few minutes zooming in and walking through each block. Study the patterns, not just the syntax.

Good luck to everyone prepping — mastery is just repetition with understanding.

text:
"I thought I knew SQL... until my interviewer asked me these!"

SQL interviews can be tricky! Here are some thought-provoking questions that tested my knowledge:

1️⃣ How do you find employees with the same salary within a department?
 2️⃣ How can you remove rows that have NULL values in specific columns?
 3️⃣ What’s the difference between INNER JOIN and CROSS JOIN?
 4️⃣ When should you use GROUP BY vs PARTITION BY?
 5️⃣ How do you find records that exist in both tables?
 6️⃣ How do you fetch the top 3 highest-paid employees in each department?
 7️⃣ How can you find employees who joined before their manager?
 8️⃣ What’s the key difference between EXISTS and IN?
 9️⃣ How would you replace specific string values in a column using SQL?
 🔟 How does the ORDER BY clause impact query performance?
 1️⃣1️⃣ How do you fetch every 5th record from a table?
 1️⃣2️⃣ What’s the difference between aggregate and analytic functions in SQL?
 1️⃣3️⃣ How do you unpivot columns into rows in SQL?
 1️⃣4️⃣ How do you calculate percentage contribution per department?
 1️⃣5️⃣ How would you identify missing sequence numbers in a column?
 1️⃣6️⃣ What’s the difference between a temporary table and a CTE?
 1️⃣7️⃣ How do you detect gaps in date ranges for each employee?
 1️⃣8️⃣ What is a correlated subquery, and when would you use it?
 1️⃣9️⃣ How do you find the most recent record for each category in a table?
 2️⃣0️⃣ How do you improve performance for a query using indexes?

SQL is powerful, but the right questions make you think beyond the basics. Which of these do you find the trickiest? Let’s discuss!

It seamlessly handles diverse content through intelligent orchestration and cross-modal understanding.

Unlike conventional RAG systems that struggle with non-textual elements, RAG-Anything delivers end-to-end multimodal processing and retrieval in one integrated framework.

📄 Universal Document Support – Process PDFs, Office docs, images, and diverse file formats

🔗 Multimodal Knowledge Graph – Extract entities and discover cross-modal relationships for deeper insights
